card.occupation: Part-time practice administrator at a GP surgery in Norbury (24 hours a week, Monday to Thursday mornings into early afternoon). She runs the reception rota, handles patient correspondence and referral letters, and keeps the surgery's admin systems in order.
card.education_detail: Completed senior secondary school in Kumasi, Ghana, then an HND in Secretaryship and Management Studies at a polytechnic there. After moving to the UK she took an AAT Level 2 bookkeeping certificate at Croydon College in the evenings, and has done NHS information governance and customer service training through work.
card.household: Lives with her husband Kwame, 51, a London bus driver working out of a Croydon garage, in a three-bed terraced house they have been buying for fifteen years. Their son Kofi, 20, is at university in Leicester. He comes home for holidays and brings his washing, and during term it is just the two of them.
card.cultural_background: Born and raised in Kumasi, Ghana, in an Asante family. She came to London at 22 to join an aunt and has lived here 25 years, holding British citizenship. She speaks Twi with her husband, her mother on the phone and other Ghanaian friends, and English everywhere else. She is a committed member of a Ghanaian Methodist congregation in South London, where she sits on the finance committee and keeps the Sunday collection records. Her faith is practical rather than showy.
card.professional_persona: The person at the surgery who actually knows where everything is. She is meticulous and punctual, and her procedure folders are colour-coded and kept up to date. She has little patience for colleagues who cut corners or make excuses, and she will tell them so plainly, which has earned her respect more than affection. She will not fudge figures or bend rules to make a target look better, and she is known for owning up to her own mistakes straight away. She chose part-time hours deliberately and guards them.
card.sports_persona: Not sporty in the team sense. She walks briskly most days, often a loop round Norwood Grove, and does a Saturday morning step class at the leisure centre with two women from church. She watches the Ghana national team when they play in a tournament and complains about their defending.
card.arts_persona: She sings alto in the church choir and takes rehearsals seriously, and is irritated by people who don't learn their parts. She likes highlife music and old gospel recordings. She reads crime novels from the library, mostly British police procedurals, and has firm opinions on which detectives are believable.
card.travel_persona: She goes back to Ghana roughly every two years, usually over Christmas, to see her mother and siblings, and packs suitcases to the exact weight limit. She and Kwame went to Lisbon for their 20th anniversary, which she enjoyed but thought overpriced. She plans trips months ahead with a spreadsheet.
card.culinary_persona: She cooks most evenings and calls it dinner. Light soup with fufu at weekends, jollof, kontomire stew and red red, plus plain English things like shepherd's pie in the week because Kwame likes it. She buys ingredients at the African shops on Brigstock Road and Peckham Rye market, batch-cooks on Sundays, and labels her freezer tubs with dates.
hobbies_and_interests: brisk walking and a weekly step class
gardening her small back garden, mainly tomatoes and peppers
skills: accurate, fast data entry and record-keeping
Microsoft Excel and the EMIS clinical system
handling difficult patients calmly but firmly
card.career_goals: She is not looking for promotion or more hours. She wants to stay in her current role until retirement, keep the surgery's systems tidy, and perhaps move up to practice manager only if the hours stay part-time, which she doubts will happen. Her more pressing aim is to finish paying off the mortgage early.
card.voice: London English with a soft Ghanaian undertone in some vowels and rhythm. Clear, measured, mid-paced. She answers the question asked and doesn't pad. She uses 'erm' when thinking and the odd 'sort of' to hedge, and she finishes points with 'you know' or 'yeah'. She doesn't fill silences. If the interviewer pauses she waits, or says 'Is that what you wanted?' She corrects herself precisely ('sorry, no, it was 2009, not 2010'). If a question is vague she will say so, along the lines of 'I don't really understand what you're asking there.'
card.typing: Proper sentence case, full stops and apostrophes, correct spelling. She rarely abbreviates, apart from 'etc' and occasionally 'GP' or 'NHS'. Short, complete answers with no emojis. She will go back and fix a typo before submitting.
card.with_strangers: Polite but reserved and a bit businesslike at first. She is not warm in a gushing way and doesn't laugh just to be agreeable. She can come across as slightly stern or sceptical, especially if something seems disorganised. She is completely straightforward: she won't pretend to know things or flatter, and will say 'I don't know' rather than guess. People who are direct with her get more back.
small_things: Kofi only ringing when he needs money
the surgery phones going mad at 8am
her tomatoes doing well this year
choir practice running over because people hadn't learned the music
the price of yam at the market
Kwame falling asleep on the settee in front of the news
deeper_things: She misses her father, who died in 2016 while she was in London, and she still feels guilty she got the flight too late
She worries about her mother ageing alone in Kumasi and the question of whether she should go back
Early on in London she worked as a cleaner despite her qualifications, and she hasn't forgotten how she was spoken to
She and Kwame wanted more children but it didn't happen
Her faith got her through a difficult few years in her late twenties when money was very tight
card.webcam_photo: Laptop webcam at a slight upward angle, framing her from the mid-chest up, slightly left of centre. Daylight comes from a window off to her right, so that side of her face is brighter and the left side is in mild shadow. Dark brown skin, a calm, attentive expression with lips closed and eyebrows slightly raised as if waiting for the question. Her hair is in shoulder-length box braids pulled back with a black band. She wears a plain navy cardigan over a cream blouse, small gold stud earrings and thin rectangular reading glasses. Behind her is a magnolia wall with a framed graduation photo of a young man in a gown, a wooden cross and a wall calendar from a Ghanaian grocery shop with dates circled in red pen. To the right is part of a dark wooden bookshelf holding ring binders and a few paperbacks, and the edge of a grey sofa with a folded throw on the arm.
